verses.text: At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went as usual into the Jewish synagogue, where they spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
So Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.
The people of the city were divided. Some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles.
But when the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them,
they found out about it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region,
where they continued to preach the gospel.
In Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet, who was lame from birth and had never walked.
This man was listening to the words of Paul, who looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed.
In a loud voice Paul called out, "Stand up on your feet!" And the man jumped up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language: "The gods have come down to us in human form!"
Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.
But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out about this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting,

"Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.
In past generations, He let all nations go their own way.
Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness."
Even with these words, Paul and Barnabas could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.
Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead.
But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. "We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God," they said.
Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.
After passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From Attalia they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had just completed.
When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they spent a long time there with the disciples.

context.author: Traditionally Luke, the physician and traveling companion of Paul
context.genre: Historical narrative — the early church's story, with speeches and eyewitness travel reports
context.audience: Theophilus, and through him a Greek-speaking readership of Jews and Gentiles
context.setting: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium until a plot to stone them forces them out. In Lystra, a city in Lycaonia, Paul heals a man lame from birth and the crowd cries out that the gods have come down. Jews arrive from Antioch and Iconium, win the crowd over, and stone Paul. He gets up, goes to Derbe, then returns through the same cities, appointing elders, and sails back to Antioch in Syria.
context.custom: The crowd speaks Lycaonian (v.11), so Paul and Barnabas do not understand what is happening until the priest of Zeus brings garlands and oxen. The people call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes because Paul does the talking. A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes once visiting the region in disguise and being turned away, which may explain the eager welcome.
context.timelineImmediate: The missionaries report to the church at Antioch how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles (v.27). That report leads straight into the debate over what Gentiles must do, in chapter 15.
context.timelineBible: Paul's short speech to pagans starts with the Creator of "heaven and earth and sea and everything in them" (v.15), the language of Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6, rather than the history of Israel he used for Jews. He appeals to rain and harvest as evidence of God's kindness.
context.sparkNotes: Paul heals a lame man in Lystra and the crowd tries to worship Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes. They stop them and point to the living God. Jews from other cities turn the crowd, and Paul is stoned and left for dead, but gets up and continues. They appoint elders in each church.

translation.meaning: The word means older men and was used for synagogue leaders. Paul appoints them in every church, with prayer and fasting, to guide the new believers.

otBackground.note: The Creator who made heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them.
The Lord who made heaven and earth and keeps faith forever.

overview.summary: In Lystra the crowd mistakes Paul and Barnabas for gods, then stones Paul. The two appoint elders in the new churches and report back to Antioch.

history.t: A rural region of central Anatolia with its own language and gods.
Lystra was a Roman colony, but many locals kept older customs.

customs.t: Priests offered sacrifices with garlands at the city gates.
A sign of grief and horror at blasphemy, as in verse 14.

archaeology.t: A Greek dedication to Zeus and Hermes was found near Lystra in 1909.
The site was identified at Kerti Höyük by an inscription found in 1956.

overview.discussion: Paul spoke differently to people with no Bible background. How do we explain the good news to someone who has no framework for it?
overview.book: The book of Acts · 28 chapters. The story of how the good news about Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome.
overview.author: Luke
